choices: Adopt whichever format the most experienced team member prefers.
Surface the competing assumptions, agree on the learner outcomes the learning must move, and select a format that can be evaluated against them.
Schedule a single after-school session so the disagreement does not delay the calendar.
Poll the team and implement the option with the most votes without reviewing evidence.
item.rationale: A disagreement about professional learning is resolved by agreeing first on the learner outcomes it must move, because format follows purpose. Naming the competing assumptions and the evidence each design would produce lets the team choose something that can actually be evaluated, rather than settling by seniority, schedule pressure, or a show of hands.

item.rationale: Beginning-practice standards ask for a design tied to a research base and to observable transfer, not for activity counts. Attendance, hours, and topic lists describe what was provided; none of them establishes whether instruction changed or whether learners benefited.

choices: Increase the number of sessions offered each term.
Replace the current provider with an outside consultant.
Move the sessions earlier in the year so more staff can attend.
Add a follow-up cycle in which participants apply the practice, receive coaching, and bring classroom evidence before the next session is planned.
item.rationale: Audits of professional learning commonly find that one-off sessions never reach instruction. The improvement that addresses that finding is a follow-up cycle with application, coaching, and evidence brought back, rather than more sessions, a different presenter, or a more convenient time, each of which adjusts delivery without adding transfer support.

choices: Assign the librarian to lead every partnership so responsibilities stay consistent.
Clarify the shared goal, then define each partner’s responsibilities, decision rights, and the review point at which the arrangement is reconsidered.
Delay the partnership until the team reaches full agreement on all details.
Let each partner define its own role independently after the work begins.
item.rationale: Disagreement about partnerships is usually disagreement about roles rather than about goals. Naming the shared goal and then fixing responsibilities, decision rights, and a review point gives the team something concrete to agree to, and makes the arrangement revisable without renegotiating it from the beginning.
choiceRationales: Not the best answer. Centralizing leadership removes the partnership rather than structuring it. choices: Recruit additional partners to broaden the program’s reach.
Publish a summary of partnership activities for the school community.
Ask each partner to submit an annual written report.
Establish a regular review in which partners examine shared evidence, adjust responsibilities, and decide whether to continue, revise, or end the arrangement.
item.rationale: A partnership weakness found in an audit is addressed by a review structure that can change the arrangement, not by expanding or publicizing it. Shared evidence together with explicit authority to revise or end the partnership is what turns a standing relationship into a managed one.

choices: Prepare one comprehensive presentation suitable for every audience.
Identify the specific decision and audience first, then select the evidence and the concrete request that fit them.
Begin with the library’s funding history so the need is understood in context.
Wait until the budget cycle closes so the message is not seen as self-interested.
item.rationale: Advocacy is shaped by the decision it is meant to influence and by who makes it. Naming the decision and the audience determines which evidence is relevant and what to ask for; a universal presentation, a historical preamble, or a delayed message each detach the communication from the decision point.

choices: Increase the frequency of newsletters sent to families.
Create a social media account dedicated to library news.
Add a library section to the school website.
Set a communication routine that reports program evidence to named audiences at the points in the year when resource decisions are actually made.
item.rationale: Advocacy weaknesses are usually about timing and audience rather than channel volume. A routine that delivers evidence to the people making resource decisions, at the moment they make them, addresses that; more newsletters, a new account, or a web page add channels without connecting to a decision point.
